import re

text = """Osteoarthritis • Skeletal dysplasia • Obesity in some cases CLINICAL FEATURES • Bowing of legs • Knees separated when 
ankles touch • Altered gait • Lateral thrust at knee • Knee pain in severe cases • Unequal loading of knee 
joint COMPLICATIONS • Medial compartment knee overload • Early osteoarthritis • Patellofemoral dysfunction • Gait 
abnormalities • Progressive deformity RADIOLOGY • Increased medial angulation • Assessment of mechanical axis • 
Growth plate abnormalities where applicable • Degenerative changes in adults CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Treat 
underlying metabolic disease • Weight management • Physiotherapy • Muscle strengthening • Gait training • Orthoses in 
selected cases SURGICAL MANAGEMENT For significant persistent/progressive deformity • Guided 
growth/hemiepiphysiodesis in growing children • Corrective osteotomy in mature patients • Knee replacement for severe 
degenerative disease --- 6 GENU VALGUM DEFINITION Genu valgum or knock knee deformity is a condition in which the 
knees approximate or touch while the ankles remain separated CAUSES • Physiological childhood valgus • Rickets • Obesity 
• Growth plate injury • Malunion • Skeletal dysplasia • Osteoarthritis • Previous trauma CLINICAL FEATURES • Knees come 
together • Ankles remain apart • Altered gait • Patellar maltracking • Knee pain • Difficulty running/walking in severe 
cases COMPLICATIONS • Patellofemoral instability • Lateral compartment overload • Early osteoarthritis • Gait 
abnormalities • Functional limitation CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Treatment of underlying cause • Weight 
management • Hip and knee strengthening • Gait training • Orthoses in selected cases SURGICAL MANAGEMENT • Guided 
growth • Distal femoral osteotomy • Corrective osteotomy • Joint replacement in severe degenerative disease --- 7 GENU 
RECURVATUM DEFINITION Genu recurvatum is a deformity in which the knee is excessively extended beyond the normal 
physiological range CAUSES • Ligamentous laxity • Neuromuscular disorders • Poliomyelitis • Quadriceps weakness • 
Anterior capsular laxity • Trauma • Malunion • Abnormal tibial slope • Poor gait mechanics CLINICAL FEATURES • 
Hyperextension of knee • Posterior displacement of knee during standing • Knee pain • Instability • Abnormal gait • 
Quadriceps weakness • Difficulty controlling knee during stance COMPLICATIONS • Chronic ligament strain • Knee 
instability • Pain • Degenerative changes • Meniscal injury • Gait dysfunction CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Quadriceps 
and hamstring strengthening • Proprioceptive training • Gait retraining • Knee brace/orthosis • Correction of underlying 
neuromuscular disorder • Activity modification SURGICAL MANAGEMENT • Ligament reconstruction where indicated • 
Corrective osteotomy • Growth modulation in selected children • Other reconstruction based on structural cause --- 8 
COXA VARA DEFINITION Coxa vara is a deformity in which the femoral neck shaft angle is reduced generally below 
approximately 120 in adults CAUSES • Congenital/developmental conditions • Rickets • Trauma • Fracture malunion • 
Fibrous dysplasia • Perthes disease • Metabolic bone disease CLINICAL FEATURES • Shortening of limb • Limp • 
Trendelenburg gait • Reduced hip abduction • Apparent shortening • Hip pain • Muscle weakness COMPLICATIONS • 
Progressive deformity • Hip instability • Early osteoarthritis • Limb length discrepancy • Abductor weakness RADIOLOGY • 
Reduced neck shaft angle • Shortened/vertical femoral neck • Altered femoral head mechanics CONSERVATIVE 
MANAGEMENT • Treat underlying metabolic disorder • Physiotherapy • Hip abductor strengthening • Gait training • 
Activity modification SURGICAL MANAGEMENT • Corrective valgus osteotomy • Internal fixation • Treatment of underlying 
bone pathology --- 9 COXA VALGA DEFINITION Coxa valga is a deformity in which the femoral neck shaft angle is increased 
generally above approximately 135 in adults CAUSES • Neuromuscular disorders • Developmental abnormalities • Hip 
dysplasia • Cerebral palsy • Muscle imbalance • Certain metabolic/skeletal disorders CLINICAL FEATURES • Reduced hip 
stability • Limp • Abductor weakness • Limited hip mechanics • Possible hip pain • Increased tendency toward subluxation 
in susceptible patients COMPLICATIONS • Hip instability • Subluxation/dislocation • Abductor insufficiency • Altered gait • 
Early degenerative changes MANAGEMENT • Treat underlying condition • Hip strengthening • Gait training • Orthotic 
management when indicated • Corrective femoral osteotomy in significant symptomatic deformity • Hip reconstruction 
when associated with instability/dysplasia --- 10 PES CAVUS DEFINITION Pes cavus is a foot deformity characterized by an 
abnormally high medial longitudinal arch often associated with plantarflexion of the first ray hindfoot varus and clawing of 
the toes CAUSES • Neuromuscular disorders • Hereditary motor sensory neuropathy • Poliomyelitis • Cerebral palsy • 
Spinal cord disorders • Trauma • Idiopathic causes CLINICAL FEATURES • High medial arch • Shortened foot appearance • 
Hindfoot varus • Claw toes • Prominent metatarsal heads • Lateral border weight bearing • Callosities • Foot pain • Ankle 
instability COMPLICATIONS • Metatarsalgia • Calluses • Ankle sprains • Plantar fascia pain • Difficulty wearing shoes • 
Progressive deformity • Gait abnormality CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Treat underlying neurological disease • Custom 
orthoses • Appropriate footwear • Stretching • Strengthening • Balance training • Gait correction • Pressure 
redistribution SURGICAL MANAGEMENT • Plantar fascia release in selected flexible deformities • Tendon transfer • 
Calcaneal osteotomy • First ray osteotomy • Midfoot osteotomy • Arthrodesis for rigid severe deformity --- 11 PES 
PLANUS DEFINITION Pes planus or flat foot is a condition in which the medial longitudinal arch of the foot is reduced or 
absent often accompanied by excessive hindfoot valgus and pronation CAUSES • Ligamentous laxity • Posterior tibial 
tendon dysfunction • Obesity • Trauma • Rheumatoid arthritis • Neuromuscular disorders • Degenerative changes • Tarsal 
coalition CLINICAL FEATURES • Flattened medial arch • Excessive pronation • Hindfoot valgus • Heel eversion • Forefoot 
abduction • Foot fatigue • Medial foot/ankle pain • Difficulty prolonged standing/walking • Abnormal shoe 
wear COMPLICATIONS • Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction • Plantar fasciitis • Ankle pain • Knee/hip biomechanical 
problems • Progressive deformity • Difficulty walking CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Weight management • Footwear 
modification • Arch support orthoses • Heel support • Stretching of tight calf muscles • Foot intrinsic strengthening • 
Posterior tibial muscle strengthening • Balance and gait training • Activity modification SURGICAL MANAGEMENT For 
symptomatic rigid/progressive deformity • Tendon reconstruction • Calcaneal osteotomy • Midfoot reconstruction • 
Arthrodesis for rigid deformity • Procedures addressing the underlying cause --- 12 HALLUX RIGIDUS DEFINITION Hallux 
rigidus is a degenerative arthritic condition of the first metatarsophalangeal joint characterized predominantly by painful 
restriction of great toe dorsiflexion CAUSES • Degenerative osteoarthritis • Previous trauma • Repetitive loading • 
Anatomical abnormalities • Inflammatory arthritis • Previous surgery CLINICAL FEATURES • Pain at first MTP joint • 
Restricted dorsiflexion • Difficulty during push off • Dorsal osteophyte • Swelling • Stiffness • Altered gait • Shoe 
discomfort COMPLICATIONS • Progressive joint degeneration • Gait alteration • Transfer metatarsalgia • Callus formation • 
Reduced walking tolerance RADIOLOGY • Joint space narrowing • Dorsal osteophytes • Subchondral sclerosis • Cystic 
changes • Advanced joint destruction CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Activity modification • NSAIDs/analgesics • Stiff 
soled shoes • Rocker bottom footwear • Orthoses • Physiotherapy • ROM exercises within tolerance • Intra articular 
injection in selected cases SURGICAL MANAGEMENT • Cheilectomy for selected early disease • Osteotomy in selected 
patients • First MTP arthrodesis for advanced disease • Joint replacement in selected patients --- 13 HALLUX 
VALGUS DEFINITION Hallux valgus is a progressive deformity in which the great toe deviates laterally toward the lesser toes 
with medial deviation of the first metatarsal producing a prominent medial eminence or bunion CAUSES/RISK FACTORS • 
Genetic predisposition • Footwear with narrow toe box • Ligamentous laxity • Pes planus • Abnormal first ray mechanics • 
Rheumatoid arthritis • Neuromuscular disorders CLINICAL FEATURES • Lateral deviation of great toe • Medial bunion • Pain 
• Redness and pressure over bunion • Difficulty wearing shoes • Callosity • Reduced first MTP movement • Transfer 
metatarsalgia • Lesser toe deformity COMPLICATIONS • Bursitis • Osteoarthritis • Metatarsalgia • Hammer/claw toes • 
Skin ulceration • Persistent gait disturbance RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES Weight bearing X ray may show • Increased hallux 
valgus angle • Increased intermetatarsal angle • Medial deviation of first metatarsal • Subluxation of first MTP joint • 
Degenerative changes CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Wide toe box footwear • Avoid tight/high heeled shoes • Bunion 
pads • Orthoses • Toe spacers in selected cases • Analgesics • Physiotherapy • Calf/foot stretching and strengthening • 
Activity modification SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Indicated for persistent pain and functional limitation despite conservative 
treatment • Distal metatarsal osteotomy • Proximal metatarsal osteotomy • Lapidus procedure in selected patients • Akin 
osteotomy • First MTP arthrodesis for severe arthritis/deformity • Bunion correction according to deformity severity --- 14 
HAMMER TOE DEFINITION Hammer toe is a deformity of a lesser toe characterized by flexion deformity of the proximal 
interphalangeal PIP joint often with relative extension at the MTP and DIP joints CAUSES • Tight footwear • Muscle 
imbalance • Hallux valgus • Pes cavus • Rheumatoid arthritis • Neurological disorders • Tendon imbalance • 
Trauma CLINICAL FEATURES • Flexed PIP joint • Pain over prominent PIP joint • Corn formation • Callosity • Difficulty 
wearing shoes • MTP pain • Reduced toe mobility • Gait difficulty in severe cases COMPLICATIONS • Corns • Ulceration • 
Infection • MTP instability • Metatarsalgia • Fixed deformity • Difficulty walking CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT • Wide toe 
box shoes • Avoid tight footwear • Toe pads • Orthoses • Splinting/taping in flexible deformity • Toe stretching • Intrinsic 
muscle strengthening • Callus care SURGICAL MANAGEMENT For painful fixed deformity • Tendon release/transfer • PIP 
joint arthroplasty • PIP arthrodesis • MTP procedures when required • Correction of associated hallux valgus/pes cavus 
--- 15 METATARSALGIA DEFINITION Metatarsalgia is a clinical condition characterized by pain and tenderness beneath the 
metatarsal heads usually caused by excessive or abnormal loading of the forefoot CAUSES • Excessive activity/running • 
Improper footwear • High heels • Pes cavus • Pes planus • Hallux valgus • Claw/hammer toes • Short or long metatarsals • 
Fat pad atrophy • Stress fracture • Inflammatory arthritis CLINICAL FEATURES • Pain beneath metatarsal heads • Burning or 
aching sensation • Pain worsens during walking/running • Forefoot tenderness • Callosity • Feeling of walking on a pebble 
• Reduced walking tolerance COMPLICATIONS • Chronic pain • Altered gait • Callus formation • Lesser toe deformity • 
Reduced physical activity • Secondary knee/hip biomechanical problems INVESTIGATIONS • Clinical examination • Weight 
bearing X ray • Ultrasound/MRI when neuroma stress fracture or soft tissue pathology is suspected CONSERVATIVE 
MANAGEMENT • Activity modification • Rest during painful period • Proper footwear with wide toe box • Metatarsal pads 
• Custom orthoses • Shock absorbing insoles • Calf and foot stretching • Foot intrinsic strengthening • Weight 
management • Analgesics/NSAIDs when appropriate SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Surgery is considered when persistent 
symptoms fail conservative treatment or when a structural cause is identified • Metatarsal osteotomy • Correction of 
associated hallux valgus • Correction of lesser toe deformity • Excision of neuroma where appropriate//////
CO 2,3 //// 1 OSTEOMYELITIS ACUTE AND CHRONIC Definition Osteomyelitis is an inflammatory and infective disease of 
bone and bone marrow usually caused by microorganisms most commonly bacteria resulting in destruction of bone and 
surrounding tissues Acute osteomyelitis Infection of bone of relatively recent onset usually associated with acute 
inflammation and systemic manifestations Chronic osteomyelitis Persistent or recurrent bone infection lasting for a 
prolonged period usually associated with necrotic bone sequestrum new bone formation involucrum sinus formation and 
recurrent discharge Common Causative Organism Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism Other organisms • 
Streptococci • Gram negative bacilli • Pseudomonas aeruginosa • Salmonella particularly in sickle cell disease • 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis tuberculous osteomyelitis Etiology / Causes 1 Hematogenous spread Microorganisms reach 
bone through the bloodstream Common in ◦ Children ◦ Metaphysis of long bones ◦ Femur ◦ Tibia ◦ Humerus 2 Direct 
implantation Organisms are introduced directly into bone following ◦ Open fractures ◦ Penetrating injuries ◦ Orthopaedic 
surgery ◦ Internal fixation ◦ Joint replacement 3 Contiguous spread Infection spreads from adjacent soft tissue Examples ◦ 
Diabetic foot ulcer ◦ Pressure sore ◦ Cellulitis ◦ Chronic wound Predisposing factors • Diabetes mellitus • 
Immunosuppression • Malnutrition • Peripheral vascular disease • Trauma • Open fracture • Previous surgery • Prosthetic 
implants • Intravenous drug use • Chronic skin infection Pathophysiology Infection → bacterial multiplication → 
inflammatory response → vascular congestion → edema → increased intraosseous pressure → vascular compromise → 
bone necrosis → abscess formation → periosteal elevation → sequestrum formation → involucrum formation → sinus 
formation Important terms Sequestrum Dead separated piece of infected bone Involucrum New bone formed around a 
sequestrum by the periosteum Cloaca Opening in the involucrum through which pus or sequestrum may discharge Clinical 
Features Acute osteomyelitis Local • Severe localized bone pain • Tenderness • Swelling • Warmth • Redness • Restricted 
movement of nearby joint • Muscle spasm Systemic • Fever • Chills • Malaise • Irritability • Tachycardia • Loss of 
appetite Chronic osteomyelitis • Persistent bone pain • Recurrent swelling • Discharging sinus • Purulent discharge • 
Recurrent fever • Non healing wound • Limb deformity • Reduced function • Local tenderness • Skin pigmentation/scarring 
• Sequestrum may occasionally be palpable Investigations Blood investigations • CBC leukocytosis in acute infection • ESR 
raised • CRP raised • Blood culture identifies causative organism • Blood glucose Imaging • X ray • Ultrasound for soft 
tissue collection • MRI highly sensitive for early osteomyelitis • CT useful for cortical destruction and sequestrum • Bone 
scan where indicated Microbiological investigation • Pus/wound culture • Bone biopsy and culture important in chronic or 
uncertain cases Complications Acute • Septicemia • Septic shock • Subperiosteal abscess • Soft tissue abscess • 
Pathological fracture • Growth disturbance in children • Joint infection Chronic • Recurrent sinus • Sequestrum • 
Involucrum • Pathological fracture • Bone deformity • Limb shortening • Secondary amyloidosis • Malignant 
transformation of chronic sinus classically squamous cell carcinoma Marjolin ulcer • Chronic pain • Functional 
disability Medical Management Acute osteomyelitis • Hospitalization when clinically indicated • Blood and tissue cultures 
• Appropriate intravenous antibiotics initially • Antibiotics modified according to culture and sensitivity • Analgesics • 
Antipyretics • Adequate hydration and nutrition • Immobilization of affected limb if necessary • Treatment of underlying 
disease Chronic osteomyelitis • Long term culture directed antibiotics • Wound care • Nutritional support • Diabetes 
control • Treatment of vascular insufficiency • Analgesia • Physiotherapy after acute infection is controlled Surgical 
Management Indications • Abscess • Sequestrum • Failure of antibiotics • Chronic sinus • Necrotic tissue • Infected 
implant • Pathological fracture Procedures • Incision and drainage • Surgical debridement • Sequestrectomy • Curettage • 
Saucerization • Removal of infected implants when appropriate • Dead space management • Bone grafting • Local 
antibiotic delivery • Soft tissue flap coverage • Stabilization of pathological fracture when required Flow Chart Infection of 
bone ↓ Inflammatory response ↓ Edema + increased intraosseous pressure ↓ Vascular compromise ↓ Bone necrosis ↓ 
Abscess / sequestrum ↓ Chronic infection ↓ Involucrum + sinus formation ↓ Debridement + antibiotics ± 
reconstruction Conclusion Osteomyelitis is a potentially destructive bone infection Early diagnosis appropriate culture 
directed antibiotics and timely drainage/debridement are essential to prevent chronic infection deformity and functional 
disability --- 2 BRODIES ABSCESS Definition Brodies abscess is a localized form of subacute osteomyelitis characterized by a 
localized intraosseous abscess usually occurring in the metaphysis of a long bone especially the tibia The common causative 
organism is Staphylococcus aureus Etiology Usually caused by • Staphylococcus aureus Predisposing factors • Previous 
minor trauma • Hematogenous infection • Reduced immunity • Diabetes • Previous inadequately treated 
infection Common Sites • Upper end of tibia common • Lower end of femur • Other long bones • Occasionally small 
bones Pathophysiology Bacterial infection ↓ Localized inflammatory response ↓ Intraosseous abscess formation ↓ 
Granulation tissue around abscess ↓ Reactive sclerosis of surrounding bone Because the infection is localized and relatively 
slow systemic manifestations may be minimal Clinical Features • Localized deep bone pain • Pain may be worse at night • 
Local tenderness • Mild swelling • Symptoms may persist for weeks or months • Fever usually absent or mild • Restriction 
of nearby joint movement may occur • Symptoms may be relieved temporarily by 
salicylates/analgesics Investigations Blood • CBC may be normal • ESR may be mildly elevated • CRP may be elevated X 
ray Typical appearance • Well defined radiolucent cavity • Surrounding sclerosis • Usually metaphyseal location MRI Shows 
• Abscess cavity • Bone marrow edema • Soft tissue involvement CT Useful for • Defining cortical involvement • Surgical 
planning Biopsy May be required to • Confirm diagnosis • Exclude tumor • Obtain culture Differential Diagnosis • 
Osteosarcoma • Ewing sarcoma • Osteoid osteoma • Chronic osteomyelitis • Bone cyst • Tuberculosis of 
bone Complications • Chronic osteomyelitis • Recurrence • Extension into soft tissues • Pathological fracture uncommon • 
Growth disturbance in children • Deformity Medical Management • Culture directed antibiotics • Analgesics • 
Rest/temporary immobilization if required • Treatment of predisposing conditions • Follow up imaging Surgical 
Management Surgery may be required when • Abscess is large • Symptoms persist despite antibiotics • Diagnosis is 
uncertain • There is extensive bone destruction • Recurrence occurs Procedures • Curettage of abscess cavity • Drainage • 
Removal of infected tissue • Cavity filling with bone graft or suitable substitute when indicated • Antibiotic therapy Flow 
Chart Subacute bacterial infection ↓ Localized bone infection ↓ Intraosseous abscess ↓ Surrounding sclerosis ↓ Persistent 
localized pain ↓ X ray/MRI diagnosis ↓ Antibiotics ± curettage/drainage Conclusion Brodies abscess should be suspected in 
patients with persistent localized bone pain and a well defined lytic lesion surrounded by sclerosis Early diagnosis prevents
progression to chronic osteomyelitis --- 3 TUBERCULOUS ARTHRITIS / TB OF SPINE AND MAJOR 
JOINTS Definition Tuberculosis of bone and joints is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium 
tuberculosis usually resulting from hematogenous spread from a primary focus commonly the lungs Tuberculosis may affect 
• Spine Potts disease • Hip • Knee • Ankle • Shoulder • Elbow • Wrist and other joints A TUBERCULOSIS OF SPINE POTTS 
SPINE Definition Potts spine is tuberculosis of the vertebral column characterized by destruction of vertebral bodies and 
intervertebral discs often leading to vertebral collapse kyphotic deformity and neurological 
complications Etiology Causative organism • Mycobacterium tuberculosis Usually spreads to the spine through • 
Hematogenous spread • Lymphatic spread • Extension from adjacent structures Common Sites • Lower thoracic spine • 
Thoracolumbar junction • Lumbar spine Pathophysiology TB infection ↓ Granuloma formation in vertebral body ↓ 
Caseous necrosis ↓ Vertebral destruction ↓ Disc involvement ↓ Vertebral collapse ↓ Kyphosis / gibbus deformity ↓ Cold 
abscess ± spinal cord compression ↓ Neurological deficit Clinical Features General • Low grade fever • Night sweats • Loss 
of appetite • Weight loss • Malaise Spinal • Persistent back pain • Local tenderness • Stiffness • Muscle spasm • Restricted 
spinal movement • Deformity • Kyphosis • Gibbus deformity Neurological • Weakness • Sensory disturbance • Radicular 
pain • Paraplegia • Bowel/bladder dysfunction in severe disease Cold abscess May appear as • Paravertebral swelling • 
Psoas abscess • Groin swelling Investigations Blood • CBC • ESR • CRP • Tuberculosis related microbiological testing as 
appropriate Imaging • X ray spine • MRI spine best for neural compression abscess and soft tissue involvement • CT bony 
destruction and surgical planning Microbiological/histological • Biopsy • Tissue culture • Molecular testing where 
appropriate Complications • Vertebral collapse • Kyphosis • Gibbus deformity • Spinal cord compression • Paraplegia • 
Nerve root compression • Cold abscess • Sinus formation • Instability • Chronic pain • Severe neurological 
disability Medical Management Anti tubercular therapy Multidrug anti tubercular therapy ATT is the cornerstone of 
treatment using an appropriate regimen according to current national/institutional guidelines Other measures • Analgesics 
• Nutritional support • Rest during active painful stage • Bracing when appropriate • Management of neurological deficits • 
Monitoring treatment response Surgical Management Indications • Progressive neurological deficit • Significant spinal cord 
compression • Severe instability • Severe or progressive deformity • Large abscess requiring drainage • Failure of 
appropriate medical treatment • Mechanical instability Procedures • Abscess drainage • Debridement • Decompression • 
Stabilization • Instrumented fusion • Corrective surgery for severe deformity B TUBERCULOUS ARTHRITIS OF MAJOR 
JOINTS Definition Tuberculous arthritis is a chronic granulomatous infection of a synovial joint caused by Mycobacterium 
tuberculosis producing synovial inflammation cartilage destruction and progressive joint damage Common Joints • Hip • 
Knee • Ankle • Shoulder • Elbow • Wrist Clinical Features The onset is generally insidious General • Low grade fever • 
Weight loss • Malaise • Reduced appetite Local • Pain • Swelling • Stiffness • Reduced range of movement • Muscle 
wasting • Joint tenderness Characteristic • A cold swelling may occur with comparatively little redness or 
warmth Advanced disease • Sinus formation • Joint destruction • Deformity • Subluxation/dislocation • Ankylosis • Limb 
shortening especially with hip disease Investigations • CBC • ESR/CRP • X ray • MRI • Ultrasound for effusion • Joint 
aspiration • Synovial fluid analysis • AFB testing/culture where appropriate • Molecular tests • Synovial biopsy Classical 
radiological findings The classical description of tuberculous arthritis includes • Periarticular osteoporosis • Peripheral 
osseous erosions • Gradual joint space narrowing Complications • Cartilage destruction • Joint deformity • Subluxation • 
Dislocation • Ankylosis • Sinus formation • Abscess • Pathological fracture • Limb shortening • Severe functional 
disability Medical Management • Appropriate multidrug ATT • Analgesics • Rest during acute painful stage • Nutritional 
support • Treatment of associated TB • Physiotherapy after acute inflammation is controlled Physiotherapy principles • 
Maintain safe joint mobility • Prevent contractures • Maintain muscle strength • Gradual functional training • Avoid 
excessive loading of a severely destroyed joint Surgical Management Depending on disease stage • Aspiration/drainage of 
abscess • Synovectomy in selected cases • Debridement • Arthrodesis for severely destroyed joints • Joint replacement in 
selected patients after adequate infection control • Spinal decompression and stabilization for Potts spine when 
indicated Conclusion TB of the spine and major joints is a slowly progressive destructive disease Early diagnosis and 
adequate ATT can prevent deformity and neurological or functional disability --- 4 PYOGENIC 
ARTHRITIS Definition Pyogenic arthritis is an acute or chronic inflammatory infection of a synovial joint caused by pyogenic 
microorganisms resulting in accumulation of infected synovial fluid/pus and potential destruction of articular cartilage The 
terms pyogenic arthritis and septic arthritis are often used interchangeably Etiology Common organisms • Staphylococcus 
aureus most common • Streptococci • Gram negative bacilli • Neisseria gonorrhoeae in appropriate populations • Other 
organisms depending on age and risk factors Routes of Infection 1 Hematogenous Most common route 2 Direct inoculation 
◦ Penetrating injury ◦ Joint injection ◦ Surgery 3 Contiguous spread ◦ Osteomyelitis ◦ Soft tissue infection ◦ Bursitis Risk 
Factors • Diabetes • Immunosuppression • Older age • Recent surgery • Joint prosthesis • IV drug use • Skin infection • Pre 
existing joint disease • Trauma Pathophysiology Bacterial entry into joint ↓ Synovial inflammation ↓ Neutrophil 
accumulation ↓ Purulent effusion ↓ Raised intra articular pressure ↓ Reduced cartilage nutrition ↓ Cartilage destruction 
↓ Subchondral bone destruction ↓ Joint deformity / ankylosis Clinical Features Acute presentation • Severe joint pain • 
Rapidly developing swelling • Warmth • Redness • Tenderness • Marked restriction of movement • Severe pain on passive 
movement Systemic • Fever • Chills • Malaise • Tachycardia Common joints • Knee • Hip • Shoulder • Elbow • 
Ankle Investigations Blood • CBC • ESR • CRP • Blood cultures Joint aspiration essential investigation Synovial fluid may 
show • Turbid/purulent appearance • High leukocyte count • Predominantly neutrophils • Gram stain • Culture and 
sensitivity Imaging • X ray • Ultrasound • MRI where required Complications • Cartilage destruction • Joint space loss • 
Osteomyelitis • Joint deformity • Ankylosis • Sepsis • Septic shock • Pathological fracture • Growth disturbance in children 
• Permanent disability Medical Management This is an orthopedic emergency • Urgent joint aspiration • Blood cultures • 
Prompt empirical antibiotics after appropriate cultures then modify according to results • Analgesics • Antipyretics • Fluid 
management if systemically ill • Treatment of underlying conditions • Temporary immobilization in the acute painful 
stage Surgical Management Main objectives • Drain pus • Reduce bacterial load • Relieve intra articular pressure • Prevent 
cartilage destruction Procedures • Needle aspiration • Arthroscopic lavage and drainage • Open arthrotomy and drainage 
when indicated • Debridement • Repeat drainage if necessary After infection is controlled • Gradual mobilization • ROM 
exercises • Muscle strengthening • Functional rehabilitation Flow Chart Bacterial invasion of joint ↓ Synovitis ↓ Purulent 
effusion ↓ Raised intra articular pressure ↓ Cartilage destruction ↓ Joint destruction ↓ Early antibiotics + drainage ↓ 
Rehabilitation Conclusion Pyogenic arthritis is a joint threatening emergency Early aspiration appropriate antibiotics and 
adequate drainage are essential to preserve joint function --- 5 SEPTIC ARTHRITIS Definition Septic arthritis is an infection 
of a joint caused by microorganisms producing inflammation and destruction of the synovium cartilage and sometimes 
subchondral bone Important examination point Pyogenic arthritis and septic arthritis are commonly used as synonyms 
Septic arthritis is the broader clinical term while pyogenic arthritis generally emphasizes bacterial suppurative 
infection Etiology Infective organisms • Staphylococcus aureus • Streptococci • Gram negative organisms • Gonococci • 
Other organisms in immunocompromised patients Routes • Hematogenous spread • Direct inoculation • Spread from 
adjacent osteomyelitis • Surgical contamination • Prosthetic joint infection Risk Factors • Diabetes mellitus • 
Immunosuppression • Rheumatoid arthritis • Prosthetic joint • Recent joint surgery • Skin infection • Intravenous drug use 
• Extremes of age • Previous septic arthritis Clinical Features Local • Severe joint pain • Swelling • Warmth • Redness • 
Tenderness • Restricted active and passive ROM • Severe pain on passive movement Systemic • Fever • Chills • Malaise • 
Tachycardia • Leukocytosis Hip septic arthritis May present with • Severe hip/groin pain • Refusal to bear weight • Painful 
hip movement • Flexion and external rotation posture in some cases Investigations Blood • CBC • ESR • CRP • Blood 
cultures Joint aspiration Most important investigation • Appearance • Cell count • Differential count • Gram stain • 
Culture and sensitivity • Crystal analysis where clinically appropriate Imaging • X ray • Ultrasound • MRI Complications •
